title: Four biggest questions facing Lamar Jackson and Ravens
summary: Despite heightened expectations of success, the Ravens have a handful of questions to answer.
full_text:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- As a first-year head coach for the Baltimore Ravens , Jesse Minter has not shied away from the championship pressures surrounding the team. 
 
 When he first stood in front of the players, Minter gave out the date, time and location of the Super Bowl. 
 
 "I know what they want to accomplish," Minter said. "I know what we've kind of set out as our goals. It's really not about anything else. And so I think you go to work every day to try to put the team in position to be able to achieve those things. We know what the standards around this place have been and where we want to go." 
 
 The oddsmakers also believe Baltimore will be among the NFL's best teams. According to DraftKings, the Ravens are tied with the Buffalo Bills for the second-best Super Bowl odds (-1000) and are tied with the Los Angeles Rams for the highest projected win total at 11.5. 
 
 But, despite the heightened expectations, the Ravens have a handful of questions to answer: 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 Who is going to be the Ravens' kicker? 
 
 
 Minter says he expects Tyler Loop to remain Baltimore's kicker heading into the season opener in Indianapolis. Beyond that, it's up to Loop's leg. 
 
 Loop missed three of eight field goal tries in the preseason, which led Baltimore to sign veteran Jake Moody to the practice squad for added competition. If Loop struggles early in the season, the Ravens can turn to Moody, who was 18-of-20 (90%) last season for the Bears and Commanders. 
 
 "We have got to make kicks," Ravens general manager Eric DeCosta said. "[It gives us a] fresh set of legs to look at, evaluate, compare, see how it all works out. In the end, it is a performance business, right? Looking at it this preseason, we decided it was probably worthwhile to bring somebody else in to see how they look." 
 
 
 Loop put together an impressive training camp, which suggested he had moved past his last-second missed kick in Pittsburgh that ended Baltimore's season. Then, even after hitting long kicks in pregame, Loop has missed from 49, 51 and 58 yards. 
 
 One of the reasons why the Ravens added Moody is because he has a strong enough leg to kick in the wintry months of the AFC North. He hit a 56-yard field goal in the Commanders' season finale in Philadelphia, where the wind chill was 28 degrees. 
 
 When Ravens special teams coordinator Anthony Levine called Loop to inform him about Moody, Loop told him, "Coach I am ready for it. I understand what is going on, and I am going to accept this challenge." 
 
 
 
 
   
 
 When will Pro Bowl defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike return? 
 
 
 The Ravens are confident that Madubuike (neck injury) will play in one of the first four games, which is why Baltimore didn't put him on injured reserve. The only uncertainty is when he will make that return. 
 
 "I am probably more bullish on that right now than I even have been," DeCosta said. "So, we feel really good about it." 
 
 Madubuike is coming back from a career-threatening neck injury that caused him to sit out the last 15 games of last season and required surgery in April. His last game was almost a full year ago -- Sept. 14. 
 
 His ramp-up to the season has been a cautious one. He has suited up for every practice of training camp but been limited to individual and positional drills. 
 
 Madubuike took another step toward returning last week, when he had a few reps in team drills. 
 
 "What that looks like for Week 1, I think it is still a day-to-day thing, I would say," Minter said. "But, we certainly have seen some things that indicate great things ahead for Nnamdi." 
    
 When Madubuike returns, Baltimore will have a formidable pass rush with him in the middle and Trey Hendrickson on the edge. From the start of 2023 until he was put on injured reserve on Sept. 27 last year, Madubuike's 21.5 sacks were the most by an NFL defensive tackle. 
 
 "I am as encouraged now as I have ever been about Nnamdi," DeCosta said. "We are very excited when we look at him and what he brings on our defense." 
 
 
 
 
 
 Who is lining up in front of quarterback Lamar Jackson ? 
 
 
 The Ravens lost three-time Pro Bowl center Tyler Linderbaum to the Las Vegas Raiders on the first day of free agency, and Baltimore still hasn't officially named his replacement. Minter said the Ravens will decide between Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic by the time the players come back Tuesday to start preparations for the season opener. 
 
 "I feel confident that we will go into game week with that pecking order for Week 1," Minter said. 
 
 
 It looked as if  Danny Pinter were closing in on the starting job before he sustained a season-ending right knee injury on Aug. 20. Gwyn is considered the front-runner after replacing Pinter with the first team, but he has played only 11 offensive snaps in three NFL seasons. Pocic is the more experienced center with 97 starts, but he is coming back from a torn Achilles that he sustained in December. 
 
 "I feel really good about how both of those guys have responded with the reps we have given them, but that is where we are at right now," Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle said. 
 
 This could be a situation in which Gwyn begins the season as the Ravens' starting center, but Pocic finishes the season as the starting center once he is more fully recovered from the Achilles injury. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Will wide receiver Rashod Bateman  be suspended? 
 
 
 DeCosta said the Ravens have received no indication on how long the NFL is going to take to investigate Bateman, who was arrested in June on family violence charges after he allegedly smashed the windshield of a car carrying his 3-month-old daughter and her mother. 
 
 Bateman is subject to discipline under the NFL's personal conduct policy, and the baseline suspension for violations involving family violence is six games. 
 
 "It is obviously something that we are very disappointed about [and] that we have to deal with these kind of things," DeCosta said. "I think right now, [it is] a little bit of a distraction at some points. ... In these matters, we just really kind of sit back and wait for the league and for the authorities to kind of tell us what is going on. We will wait." 
 
 Bateman, who is the Ravens' No. 2 wide receiver, continues to practice with the team. If Bateman sits out any time, it would mean an increased role for Ja'Kobi Lane , a rookie third-round pick who was the star of training camp. 
 
 "We feel like we have got a young group of receivers -- a bunch of guys that can make plays," DeCosta said. "[I am] excited about that. We will just have to wait and see what happens."

title: 2026 NFL season sim: Predictions, surprises, playoff teams
summary: We played out one of the Football Power Index's 10,000 season simulations (No. 9,187), from Week 1 through Super Bowl LXI.
full_text:
Every preseason, we forecast possibilities for how the upcoming NFL season could pan out. Which teams  might emerge? Which teams  could go on a run? And which teams  should win the Super Bowl?

 But today is a day for absolutes. ESPN's  Football Power Index  simulates the season thousands of times to build our projections  ... but what if we look at only one simulation from the set? Just one possible outcome, one way things could play out. Life is a single simulation, after all.

 To be clear, what follows is neither my predictions nor the prognostications of ESPN Analytics. This is simply the story of simulation No. 9,187. Let's see how it plays out (with a little creative license woven in).

 See FPI's projections for the 2026 season 

 

 

 Hype on Bears and Texans falls very flat 
 These teams have been trendy preseason picks to go on deep playoff runs. But they didn't just miss the postseason in this simulation -- they weren't even close.

 

 For the Bears, it became apparent by midseason that the hoped-for growth in Year 2 under Ben Johnson wasn't going to happen. They were 3-6 through Week 10, with quarterback Caleb Williams still struggling with accuracy and the running game not enjoying the efficiency it showed in 2025.

 Houston's story was different. The Texans were 6-3 and firmly in the playoff race through 10 weeks, a game behind the Jaguars in the AFC South. But the version of C.J. Stroud we saw against the Patriots in the 2025 divisional playoffs  emerged in the second half of the season. And Houston's vaunted defense fell off dramatically, too. The result? An improbable eight-game losing streak to finish the season.

 Chicago and Houston sported 6-11 records, with both teams' fanbases focused on their top-10 picks in the 2027 NFL draft rather than the playoff runs they expected entering the season.

 
 

 Cowboys win a mediocre NFC East 
 With two weeks left, the Cowboys, Eagles and Giants were in a three-way tie with mediocre 7-8 records. It took weeks for Philadelphia to find its offensive rhythm under new coordinator  Sean Mannion. The Cowboys' new-look defense held up well early in the season but couldn't sustain that improvement, causing Dallas to enter the final two weeks on a four-game losing streak. The Giants' passing game struggled early with wide receiver Malik Nabers being limited but got better as he got healthier.

 All three teams had a shot at the playoffs with two games left. The Cowboys dealt a major blow to New York in Week 17, winning a 19-7 defensive battle. The Eagles upset the 49ers 23-19 on the road. But the Cowboys had the tiebreaker advantage, so Dallas took the division when it beat the Commanders in Week 18 even though Philadelphia prevailed over the Giants to finish with an identical 9-8 record.

 Dallas got the No. 4 seed in the NFC playoffs as the division winner with the worst record while the Eagles missed out. That earned the Cowboys a home wild-card game against the fifth-seeded, defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks. Dak Prescott lit up Seattle's defense, throwing two touchdowns to CeeDee Lamb in a 31-19 victory that had Cowboys fans dreaming of a trip to the Super Bowl.

 But it was not to be. The Cowboys lost 27-20 to the Lions in Detroit a week later to fall short of the conference championship round yet again.

 

 
 

 Chiefs retake the AFC West, Broncos miss the playoffs 
 The Chiefs won the AFC West nine seasons in a row from 2016 to 2024 and made three consecutive Super Bowls before a wildly disappointing 2025 campaign in which they finished 6-11 and missed the playoffs. Kansas City got back on top in 2026 -- of the division, at least.

 It was almost a wire-to-wire performance. The Chiefs took sole possession of first place after Week 4 and never gave it up despite the Chargers' best efforts. Patrick Mahomes rebounded to some degree, returning to being a top-five QBR passer but not the MVP. And receiver Rashee Rice finally achieved the full season of success that had previously eluded him.

 The 12-5 Chiefs earned the No. 2 seed in the AFC, with the Chargers making the playoffs as the No. 5 seed at 10-7. The Chargers got the last laugh, though, beating Kansas City 27-24 at Arrowhead Stadium in the divisional playoffs.

 As for the Broncos, who were arguably a Bo Nix injury short of making it to the Super Bowl a year ago? They regressed badly and finished 7-10.

 
 

 Patriots, Steelers fail to reach the postseason 
 The Patriots looked like they were going to back up their status as reigning AFC champions, sporting a 6-3 record and a 1½-game lead in the AFC East through Week 9. But New England stumbled against some heavy hitters, losing to the Lions, Chargers, Bills, Vikings and Broncos in the back half of the season. That resulted in a 9-8 record, which was not good enough for a wild-card spot, as the Pats lost tiebreakers to the Colts and Bengals.

 Pittsburgh also fell short in its first season under Mike McCarthy , missing the playoffs for the first time since 2022. Quarterback Aaron Rodgers was below average again, and the rest of the roster wasn't strong enough to make up for it, so the Steelers limped to an 8-9 record.

 

 
 

 Jaguars take the AFC South, but Colts steal their thunder 
 Jacksonville came out of the gates hot, with quarterback Trevor Lawrence picking up right where he left off in 2025. The Jaguars started the season 7-2 and pulled away after Houston imploded, clinching the division by Week 16. The Jaguars lost their final two games to finish 10-7 but safely made the playoffs as the No. 3 seed.

 Jacksonville earned the right to face division foe Indianapolis at home in the wild-card round. The Colts got into the playoffs by beating a Jaguars team that was resting its starters in Week 18 and repeated the feat against Jacksonville's A-team, shutting down Lawrence and the Jags' offense to win 18-12.

 It was a 180-degree reversal for Indianapolis, which lost its last seven games in 2025 to go from 8-2 to out of the playoffs. But the Colts' Cinderella run in 2026 ended with a 55-23 loss to top-seeded Buffalo in the divisional playoffs.

 
 

 Panthers start 0-7, but Jets earn the No. 1 draft pick 
 The Bryce Young era in Carolina ended at some point during the team's seven-game, season-opening losing streak. He's under contract for next year, but it became clear that Carolina was going to need to find another quarterback -- perhaps in the 2027 draft. But it won't be with the first pick. The Panthers played three different quarterbacks during the back half of the season and finished with a 6-4 burst to go 6-11, ending with the No. 4 pick.

 The honor of selecting first went to the Jets, who finished two games behind everyone else in going 2-15. So will the Jets draft  Arch Manning with the first pick? Dante Moore ? CJ Carr ? Darian Mensah ? Drew Mestemaker ? Trinidad Chambliss ? Someone else? New York is spoiled for choice, especially given its three first-round picks.

 
 

 Exceptional NFC West comes down to the wire ... 
 The NFC West boasts  three of FPI's top five teams entering 2026. Those preseason expectations came to fruition in simulation 9,187.

 Through 12 weeks, the Seahawks, 49ers and Rams were each 9-2 -- with only three of those six combined losses coming to teams outside the division! Fast forward to Week 18, with the 49ers and Seahawks entering their finales tied at 12-4 and the Rams one game back at 11-5. But the Rams came out firing in Week 18, blowing out the Seahawks 37-8. The 49ers destroyed the last-place Cardinals 30-3, securing not only the division but also the No. 1 seed in the NFC. Seattle and Los Angeles had to settle for the No. 5 and No. 6 seeds, respectively.

 So that had the 49ers feeling good entering the playoffs. Was this the year Kyle Shanahan and San Francisco would get over the Super Bowl hump?

 

 
 The Rams get the last laugh ... to an extent 
 All three NFC West stalwarts were considered Super Bowl contenders entering the…

title: Bears' offseason party is over as toughest schedule looms
summary: Chicago has eight games against teams that made the '25 playoffs, so the time to celebrate last season is over.
full_text:
LAKE FOREST, Ill. -- This season marks a bittersweet 10th anniversary for Chicago Bears defensive tackle Grady Jarrett , whose 2016 season with the Atlanta Falcons brought the greatest moment -- and heartbreak -- of his career.

 That season ended with Jarrett playing in his first and so far only Super Bowl. He had a game-high three sacks of New England Patriots legend Tom Brady, but Jarrett doesn't celebrate the historic nature of that game. The game featured the greatest comeback in Super Bowl history as the Patriots overcame a 28-3 deficit to win 34-28 in overtime.

 But if there's one positive takeaway Jarrett could use to teach his current teammates, it's this: The Falcons entered that season with the toughest strength of schedule in the NFL. That's the challenge the Bears face, beginning with Sunday's opener on the road against the defending NFC South champion Carolina Panthers (1 p.m. ET, Fox).

 "It's just a testament to how hard we worked last season to be able to have the opportunity to have the quote-unquote hardest schedule," Jarrett said. "We've got a lot of primetime games [five]. People want to see us play.

 "When we go out there and play, we've got to give them a show."

 Chicago faces four division champs this season, including the Panthers. The Bears also take on the defending Super Bowl and NFC West champion Seattle Seahawks , NFC East champs Philadelphia Eagles and AFC South champion Jacksonville Jaguars .

 The Bears' foes had a .550 winning percentage last season, and eight of Chicago's 17 games will be against playoff teams.

 If coach Ben Johnson needed evidence for why the Bears can't rest on their laurels after an 11-6 finish and NFC North title in 2025, that schedule should help. Also, over the past 15 seasons, only the 2013 Panthers, 2015 Pittsburgh Steelers , 2016 Falcons, 2021 Steelers and 2023 Eagles made the playoffs after facing the league's hardest schedule.

 "You know, the Chicago Bears are such an iconic franchise, and it's great the Chicago Bears being back in the playoffs and being able to get in the playoffs, get a win, win the NFC North, but there's still more things to achieve," said Bears guard Joe Thuney , a four-time Super Bowl champ with the Kansas City Chiefs . "And obviously, there are a lot of cool moments last year, but I don't think anybody in this building is satisfied. I don't think anybody's relaxing on that or resting on that.

 "And I think that's what's so cool is, there's still a very, very, strong burning hunger and desire to push more and keep going, keep improving. So, there's a lot still left to do."

 The Bears' offseason featured videos of fans celebrating the team's first playoff win since 2011 in a commercial for United Airlines that ran for months. Bears chairman George H. McCaskey was repeatedly watching the viral mashup of Caleb Williams ' overtime winner against the Packers set to the tune of Celine Dion's "My Heart Will Go On."

 Williams made the EA Sports Madden NFL 27 cover , and the Bears have been a feel-good story. But the celebrations and that schedule, and the history of teams facing such a gauntlet, made Johnson wary. DraftKings Sportsbook was also wary and projected a third-place Bears finish in the NFC North, behind the  Detroit Lions and Green Bay Packers .

 "Are you trying to annoy me right now?" Johnson said when asked about 2025 once more during a late August joint practice with the Tennessee Titans .

 "Talking about last year isn't going to do us any good in terms of winning this practice, winning the next preseason game, winning Week 1, and that's really all we care about right now."

title: C.J. Stroud confident ahead of the biggest season of his life
summary: After a rocky end in the playoffs last season, it appears Stroud will play Year 4 without a new contract.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- Quarterback C.J. Stroud sported a large white T-shirt and baggy gray shorts as he drove to Reliant Stadium around 7 a.m. on July 28. He casually strolled into the  Houston Texans ' facility, reporting for his fourth training camp while the team's social media crew recorded his arrival.

 Minutes later, they posted the video on X, and the clip spread like a contagion across social media -- generating over 20 million views and sparking feedback about Stroud's "back-to-school" look.

 Stroud, who has family and close friends run his accounts, tries to avoid scrolling on social media, but even a post from "Maxisnicee," who reenacted Stroud's training camp entrance, got a reaction out of Stroud -- who posted laughing emojis under the Instagram video.

 "Max, that's my boy. I was tired," Stroud told ESPN with a laugh. "I was focused on doing my job and getting better that day, not what I was wearing. Sometimes you can't in life be super hard on yourself. ... I laugh at a lot of stuff because it's funny."

 

 Although the entrance to the building inspired jokes, the fact remains that Stroud is entering a pivotal Year 4. He hopes to play well enough to wash away the memories of last year's playoff struggles. According to DeMeco Ryans, the offseason and training camp were an excellent start -- with the Texans' coach saying Stroud "handled himself tremendously."

 "He's done a really good job of commanding the offense," Ryans said. "Great job of communicating with everyone, offensive line, receivers, tight ends, running backs. He's done a great job just having all those guys together, leading, speaking up in meetings, doing all those things you expect from your starting quarterback."

 That's Step 1 for Stroud, whose contract situation has been a talking point this offseason, but ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported Wednesday that "the current sentiment is Stroud will most likely not end up with a new deal" before Sunday's season opener.

 All of that should become clear this week after a deadline was set.

 "If we don't get it figured out before the season starts, then it'll be something we address in the offseason," general manager Nick Caserio said.

 The season starts against the Buffalo Bills , and according to league sources, both sides are content with Stroud's lack of a contract extension. It gives the Texans an extra year of evaluation and allows Stroud to bet on himself.

 Houston picked up Stroud's fifth-year option of his rookie deal in April, so he's still under contract in 2027. If he can get back to the trajectory he showed as a rookie, he could eventually sign a record-setting deal.

 Houston has shown that it will invest in its players, resetting the market with cornerback Derek Stingley Jr . (2025), and Will Anderson Jr . this offseason, which made him the highest-paid non-QB in NFL history .

 It's not a secret, however, that if Stroud struggles, questions about his future in Houston will continue.

 "Pressure is a privilege," Stroud said. "I'm excited. I've always been challenged in my career. I've always had to persevere through things, and I think this is something that I'm grateful for. I didn't wake up and forget how to play football."

 

 

 A DOWNPOUR OF scrutiny has rained down on Stroud since the Texans' season-ending loss to the New England Patriots in the divisional round of the playoffs.

 His four-interception performance (all in the first half) birthed offseason chatter ranging from whether Houston should trade him or pay him .

 Criticism isn't rare to Stroud, having learned to deal with it since his days at Ohio State. He has developed ways to ignore the noise, but something as simple as picking up his phone can open a gateway to negativity because of things such as social media.

 

 "People are quick to use Twitter," Stroud said. "I focus on me. I can't control [social media], so why would I care? Of course I'm human. I learned if some people had the opportunity to be me, they would. But a lot of people have opinions and don't have opportunities.

 "So the more opinions people have, the more opportunity that I have to prove who I am. They love to critique. That's part of life. I play in an entertainment sport, so they're critical of a lot of people. I have the opportunity to go play. No one can stop that."

 It will take a strong season to remove the stench from his last playoff game. But he feels he has been able to navigate the aftermath -- in part because it reminded him that failure doesn't define him.

 "I'm proud of myself for how I've handled these past couple months," Stroud said. "Yeah, I have things that I want back and mistakes that I made. But truly, God has worked through my shortcomings. If I was perfect, I wouldn't be able to be coachable or have the fear of God. So I'm glad that I have made mistakes."

 Through the scrutiny, Stroud's teammates have galvanized around their quarterback, as they know they'll need him at his best for a potential Super Bowl run.

 "He's built for everything," wide receiver Nico Collins told ESPN. "We believe in him, we love him. This is the best position he can be in right now. I feel like he is about to go out and show the whole world what he's made of, and I can't wait. We got his back 100%, all the way."

 

 
 SINCE A HISTORIC rookie season, Stroud's play has careened between flashes of brilliance and stretches of frustration. It has led to this crossroads of what to pay Stroud, and when to pay him. Stroud, though, has left negotiations to his agent, David Mulugheta, and has zeroed in on football.

 "You have to keep the main thing the main thing," Stroud said the day after his viral video was posted. "You have to just focus on one day at a time, one play and the football is what's gotten me to even have the conversation, to be able to get a second contract. I have to focus on football."

 

 Stroud ended 2023 as the Offensive Rookie of the Year, and he earned a Pro Bowl selection after throwing for 4,108 yards (the third most by a rookie in NFL history) and 23 touchdowns against just five interceptions.

 The yards and touchdowns were career highs. The interceptions were a career low. Yet it almost feels ancient.

 In 2024, he had 3,727 passing yards with 20 touchdowns and 12 interceptions. In 2025, he finished with 3,041 passing yards, 19 touchdowns and eight interceptions.

 Things weren't all negative though, as ESPN Analytics had him with the fifth-lowest turnover rate, 11th-best QBR and eighth-best expected points added per dropback (.19) last season. He also hasn't missed the playoffs since entering the league, and each year, the Texans have won their playoff opener.

 But going into 2026, Houston feels like it's a Super Bowl contender -- despite never advancing past the divisional round -- behind one of the league's best defenses.

 "Every year we always go short of that third round," Collins said. "I feel like this year, it's time to take that leap and go where we need to go."

 

 THE TEXANS BELIEVE the playcalling should be improved in Year 2 under offensive coordinator Nick Caley, with Houston ranking 18th in total offense (327 yards) and 16th in offensive points per game (21.9) last season.

 During training camp, Caley said, "I want to give ourselves an opportunity to play our best football when it matters the most." It's a reference to the playoffs where he and his quarterback must rise to the occasion.

 The synergy between quarterback and playcaller is vital. In June, Caley said he and Stroud have been able to "dive deeper" into their working relationship, and throughout camp he felt Stroud's process was stellar and that he was "even-keeled every day."

 "The ability to move on from a good play to the next play, a bad play to the next play, Stroud's demeanor has been awesome," Caley said. "His approach, his process, it's been consistent. It's really been consistent since spring, and I'm proud of him."

 Caserio echoed that sentiment in the spring.

title: NFL division, conference and Super Bowl best bets for 2026 season
summary: Who's winning the Super Bowl? Which teams are winning their divisions and conferences? Our analysts offer their best bets.
full_text:
A lot has changed since the end of last season and  Week 1 of this season. And you can be sure much more will change between now and Super Bowl Sunday.

 Entering last season, the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks were both 60-1 to win the Super Bowl. The Patriots were as long as 120-1 after Week 3. We know how that all worked out.

 

 Heading into the 2026 season, the Los Angeles Rams are the Super Bowl favorite at +500, with a sizable gap between them and the Baltimore Ravens (10-1), Buffalo Bills (10-1) and the defending champion Seahawks (12-1). Following the top four, 10 teams have odds from 16-1 to 20-1.

 Looking at divisions, among teams that missed the playoffs last season but are favored to win their division are the Ravens, Kansas City Chiefs , Detroit Lions , Tampa Bay Buccaneers . The only team that won its division last year and is favored to do so again is the Philadelphia Eagles in the NFC East.

 The Rams are the favorites to win the NFC, and the Ravens have the shortest odds in the AFC, followed closely by the Bills.

 So, how do we bet these teams? We asked our analysts to break down the odds and offer their best bets.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change .

 
 Sign up for ESPN Fantasy Football . Play the No. 1 fantasy game for free! 

 

   Detroit Lions to win NFC North (+175) 
 Pamela Maldonado:  Detroit has real flaws, especially along an offensive line that never fully recovered from losing its veteran core. But the schedule gives the Lions a major rebound opportunity. They project to face the NFL's easiest schedule, including the easiest slate of run defense, which sets up perfectly for Jahmyr Gibbs . Detroit went 9-8 last season despite brutal injury and fumble luck. With better health and typical regression, the Lions should look more like their winning selves. In Green Bay, Micah Parsons ' early absence leaves too much of the season resting on Jordan Love and the offense to carry an average defense, while the Bears' defense will learn if it can hold up if it can't duplicate the turnover magic that fueled last year's success. That leaves +175 for the Lions worth backing.

   Houston Texans  to win Super Bowl (18-1) 
 

 Matt Bowen:  We have to start with the defense in Houston. It's a championship-caliber unit that allowed the second-fewest points per game last season (17.4), and we know DeMeco Ryans has the pass rushers to close out games. But we also have to look at the offensive side of the ball. The Texans traded for running back David Montgomery and upgraded the offensive line. If Houston can run the ball with serious efficiency and create more positive situations for quarterback C.J. Stroud as a passer, this team can go on a real run.

  Texans to win AFC (+870) 
 Joe Fortenbaugh: Houston is priced like a team with an elite defense but a lousy quarterback. So, I ask you this: What happens if Stroud is average this season? Better yet, what happens if Stroud is above average this season? Imagine competent quarterback play, much like Stroud exhibited during his rookie season, to go alongside what very well might be the league's nastiest defense? This is a value play, as we're buying low on Stroud.

   Jacksonville Jaguars to win AFC (15-1) 
 Ben Solak: The Texans are almost twice as likely to win the conference (+870) as the Jaguars, and they have a big edge in the division as well (+105 to +245). I don't think the margin is that big between the two, and I like Jacksonville divisional and conference bets accordingly. But by weighted DVOA, which prefers recent games to long past games, the Jaguars were the third-best team in football and best in the AFC -- the Texans were fifth and second, respectively. Houston made the bigger offseason additions in S Reed Blankenship and OGs Wyatt Teller and Keylan Rutledge , but it has also endured the bigger offseason injury (WR Jayden Higgins , torn right ACL). On a neutral field, my numbers and my heart both think Houston is the better team -- but it's by a slim margin.

   Minnesota Vikings to win NFC North (+450) 
 Solak: I power rate the NFC North very closely across the board, and the Vikings are listed as a clear fourth in the divisional odds -- so that's where I want my money. Kyler Murray is an average starting quarterback. Since entering the league, he's dead average by dropback success rate (47.2%) and EPA per dropback (0.08). His QBR is 12th among 40 qualifying quarterbacks! Kevin O'Connell's Vikings, as long as they have average quarterback play, deliver winning seasons thanks to a highly explosive passing attack and opportunistic defense. Even if the departures of LB  Jonathan Greenard  and S Harrison Smith slow down the Vikings' playmaking on defense, much of their magic is the result of Brian Flores' scheming, which is still in the building. Minnesota should be in the mix for the division the whole way.

   New England Patriots  to win Super Bowl (18-1) 

 Liz Loza:  The schedule has stiffened, but so has the squad. New England spent the offseason methodically building around budding superstar Drake Maye by trading for deep threat A.J. Brown and receiver Romeo Doubs . Running back  TreVeyon Henderson returns for his second year to give balance to the ground game, while new offensive line investments figure to protect the Patriots' franchise QB. On defense, the addition of safety Kevin Byard should buoy the secondary, while defensive end Dre'Mont Jones strengthens the pass rush. Mike Vrabel has already changed the culture in New England. His partnership with Josh McDaniels provides the Patriots with the collective leadership needed to build on last year's momentum, further converting the roster's talent into postseason success.

   Philadelphia Eagles  to win Super Bowl (17-1) 
 Eric Moody:  Philadelphia is an intriguing pick at these odds. The Eagles are just two years removed from a championship, have reached three Super Bowls since 2017 and face the league's seventh-easiest schedule based on 2026 win totals, with many of their toughest games coming on their home field. Jalen Hurts , Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith give the offense plenty of firepower, while Vic Fangio leads a defense that allowed the sixth-fewest points last season. This roster is capable of another deep postseason run, and the price is appealing.

title: Life after football: Joshua Kelley's path to filmmaking after the NFL
summary: We caught up with former Chargers player Joshua Kelley about life and filmaking after his NFL career.
full_text:
SINCE JOSHUA KELLEY  was 8 years old, his life was almost all about football.

 He finally started living out his dream of playing in the NFL when the Los Angeles Chargers selected him in the fourth round of the 2020 draft out of UCLA. Through four seasons with the Chargers, Kelley was a rotational running back and special teams contributor, totaling 1,148 yards and two touchdowns.

 When his rookie contract expired, Kelley joined the New York Giants for training camp then the Tennessee Titans for the 2024 season. As the season went on, however, he began to realize his priorities had changed. On team plane rides his mind was elsewhere, often in some alternate universe he'd created in his notebook. He began to dread team meetings, wanting to instead stay in his hotel room and write out the scenes of movies that cycled through his head.

 

 "That's when I kind of knew it was kind of done for me," Kelley told ESPN. "When that Sunday morning, that jittery, feeling kind of was not there anymore."

 Kelley hasn't officially retired from the NFL yet -- he jokes that he is keeping the door open just in case -- but as the 2026 campaign is set to kick off, he is transitioning into a new season of his own, as a filmmaker. Kelley, 28, wrote, directed and self-financed two short films this summer, one of which stars his former Chargers teammate  Keelan Doss . Kelley's first film, " No Chaser , " premiered Aug. 29 on YouTube.

 As Kelley's playing career reached its conclusion, he had something of an identity crisis, but through filmmaking he has found a new purpose, and he hopes to give that to other former players.

 "For us as football players, just athletes in general, once we're done playing, it's scary," Kelley said. "I just wanted to show athletes that it's possible to pivot and do your thing."

 

 A LARGE PART of Kelley's childhood was spent at the movie theater with his brother, Daniel, watching Spider-Man or other superhero films. When he wasn't at the theater, he was watching animated shows including "Naruto," "Dragon Ball Z" and "One Piece" and playing video games such as Final Fantasy, Kingdom Hearts and The Legend of Zelda.

 Kelley describes his hometown of Lancaster, California, as "the middle of nowhere," but these alternate realities allowed him to be anywhere he wanted to be.

 "It just kind of worked my brain," he said. "It's like a muscle that I developed over time, and then that love for it just came out to creative writing."

 But those creative muscles always took a back seat to football -- until Kelley didn't have football anymore.

 

 After the 2023 NFL season, Kelley was excited about what was next. His rookie contract was ending, meaning he was entering free agency for the first time, and he had an opportunity to potentially choose where he'd land.

 But Kelley went seven months without suiting up for an NFL team. At his home in Los Angeles, he felt a mix of embarrassment and confusion about his identity.

 "It gets real. All of a sudden, the people that are blowing up your line every day to congratulate you after the game, they're not doing that anymore," he said.

 "I was going through something, and I was like, 'Dang, who am I?'"

 While he was waiting for a call from an NFL team, Kelley's screenwriting journey began in earnest. His life was different without having to be at mandatory team offseason programming, allowing him to spend more time with his wife, Mikaela, and his son, Elijah. (The Kelleys now have another son, Caleb, who was born in April.) Still, Kelley set aside a few hours each day to write.

 "He would always be like, 'Look, I need to go in the room, be by myself and write,'" Mikaela said. "'During that time, I'd be like, 'Dude, what are you even working on?'"

 

 Kelley was excited to return to the NFL in October 2024 when he signed with the Titans, and he remained in Tennessee throughout the rest of the season. He didn't see much playing time, appearing in just three games and getting one carry for 2 yards, but his writing journey continued in the background.

 It was with Tennessee, on the team planes, in hotels and even in the locker room, where Kelley wrote an entire series about a football player going through a mental health crisis. Kelley wrote about 4,000 pages over the course of that year using his and friends' experiences to create the comedy-drama.

 That exploratory script ended up getting Kelley his first taste of Hollywood.

 After Kelley's agent, Bill Douglas at the entertainment and sports agency Paradigm, saw the script, he forwarded it to Dan Fogelman, Jess Rosenthal and Kevin Falls, the executive producers of an upcoming Hulu TV series, "The Land." The show is focused on a family involved in the Cleveland Browns organization, and they were looking for writers with professional football experience.

 "We really liked his scenes that were off the football field," Falls told ESPN. "You really get the feeling of a young couple and everyone thinks, 'Oh, that's a glamorous life.' And many times it is, but you get to see all of it."

 Kelley joined "The Land" as an entry-level staff writer in February 2025, shortly after the Titans' season ended. For the next five months, he helped shape key elements of the show. One character, Zeke, is modeled after Kelley's life. Kelley crafted most of Zeke's story, which includes the tension that comes with life outside of football: navigating media, marriage and personal life.

 "Most writers at the lower levels get rewritten extensively, sometimes higher levels too, but Joshua contributed," Falls said. "Joshua will have the pride of ownership when he sees his episode and know, 'Hey, that's me. I wrote that.'"

 That experience helped give Kelley something of a blueprint to what he'd do months later.

 
 

 INSIDE THE CASA Rios Mexican restaurant, which sits in the shadows of SoFi Stadium where Kelley played for four years with the Chargers, he was trying to finish his second film, "Leverage," without needing an extra day -- and potentially spending thousands of more dollars.

 And he was running out of time.

 "How much time do you think this scene will take?" Elena Lozonschi, an assistant director, asked Kelley.

 "About 15 minutes"

 "Can you make it 10?"

 "Sure."

 Mikaela, who had been juggling producing and breastfeeding the then 3-month-old Caleb throughout the day, handed their baby to Alex Van Dyke, Kelley's former UCLA football teammate who is in the film, and began helping by grabbing cups for a kitchen scene. Kelley ran into the back of the restaurant to help with the setup for a scene.

 In the end, Kelley got all the scenes done. The crisis was avoided, but the adrenaline rush from tense moments like that or from getting a scene to come to life exactly as he envisioned it is the closest he has gotten to the jitters he once felt from playing in the NFL.

 "I'm still kind of chasing that through filmmaking a little bit, that adrenaline rush," he said. "I feel like through filmmaking, being on set, this sort of feels again like I'm back in another playing field."

 On this playing field, Kelley has more control than he ever had as a player, when his success depended on the playcall, the quarterback and how the offensive line blocked.

 After Kelley yelled "Action!" to begin a scene, he closely watched Doss perform a scene at a table counter, but he quickly yelled, "Cut!" Kelley realized Doss' chain wasn't positioned correctly to match a previous scene and gave other directives before heading into the next scene.

 "I feel like that's why I gravitate towards this because I'm just like, I'm really in control of my destiny," he said. "I love this freedom."

 

 Kelley experienced that freedom for the first time earlier this summer while shooting "No Chaser." Kelley's goal, he said, is to make the viewer feel like they've watched something they've never seen before.

title: Mike Vrabel emerged from his offseason scandal. Its effects linger
summary: Mike Vrabel and the New England Patriots moved past the Dianna Russini scandal. Others are still feeling its effects.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Mike Vrabel, the hulking former linebacker who coached his team to the Super Bowl last season, had assumed his news conference power stance: arms stretched wide to grab the lectern in front of him. It was a morning in August ahead of New England Patriots training camp practice. The head coach wore his trademark blue vest and white long-sleeved shirt.

 "What did you learn from counseling?" a reporter asked.

 Vrabel dodged the question about the scandal that rocked the NFL offseason. Instead, he turned his answer into a discussion about New England's offensive line: "I just walked into that meeting room and said, 'How do we improve? How do we improve our combination blocks?"

 He spoke for one minute and six seconds. He never mentioned the word counseling.

 

 Vrabel was the feel-good story of last NFL season as he led the Patriots from 4-13 to the Super Bowl in his first year coaching his former team.

 But after the New York Post in April published photos of him and former Athletic NFL reporter Dianna Russini together at an adults-only resort, he became a fascination beyond just sports media, crossing over into the tabloids. The attention grew so intense that Vrabel stepped away from the team to seek counseling. Vrabel's future was debated across sports media. NFL observers and personnel wondered aloud if the scrutiny on his personal life would grow into a problem on the field.

 As a new season of Super Bowl expectations begins, Vrabel's close connection to players and his track record of success have allowed him to move beyond the offseason scandal in the locker room and organization. At the same time, aftershocks continue to ripple through the league, from team front offices to the coaching ranks, in some cases changing how men who work in the league interact with women who report on it.

 ESPN spoke with league insiders, reporters, players and coaches, most of whom spoke only on the condition of anonymity, about the Patriots' offseason and how the Vrabel-Russini situation impacted the league.

 One woman who covers the NFL said that an assistant coach said he wouldn't want to be seen meeting with her because of the optics after the Vrabel scandal. Several women reporters and coaches told ESPN they are more cautious now when interacting with each other because they feel more closely watched. They worry about the league's annual scouting combine in March, an event defined by late-night intermingling between team personnel and reporters at bars that helps define coverage for fans.

 The Patriots declined to make Vrabel available for an interview and declined to comment for this story. In New England, multiple Patriots personnel and players followed Vrabel's lead, declining requests to discuss how they navigated the offseason, and those who did talk shared few details. The team offered two players -- running back Rhamondre Stevenson and safety Kevin Byard -- to speak to ESPN. "We just tried to move on as fast as we can from that," Stevenson said.

 At training camp, a group of players' and coaches' wives and girlfriends were watching practice when ESPN approached one coach's wife to discuss the strange offseason. "I love chatting," she said, "if it were any other topic."

 "We love this team, and the Pats stick together," she continued. "That's all I'll say."

 

 

 VRABEL RECEIVED A  call from a New York Post reporter on Easter Sunday regarding the photos that showed him and Russini hugging and interlocking fingers at the resort, according to a person with knowledge of the call.

 Vrabel told Page Six that the photos "show a completely innocent interaction and any suggestion otherwise is laughable." According to a person who spoke to Vrabel at the time, the head coach had wanted to issue a stronger statement that defended Russini's reporting ethics but settled on downplaying the photos.

 Russini resigned from The Athletic less than a week later. (The Athletic ultimately found that Russini's relationship with Vrabel violated its newsroom standards but that her coverage did not show a clear bias. She declined to comment for this story.) When Vrabel met reporters for the first time on April 21, he seemed chastened as he told the assembled media he'd "had some difficult conversations" with people that he cared about. He decided to miss the third day of the NFL draft to seek counseling. It was around that time that one team source noticed Vrabel was quieter than normal and not walking around the facility greeting everyone he passed as he normally would.

 The chaos continued over the following weeks as tabloids published more old photos of him together with Russini (they are both married to other people). Page Six even published photos of Vrabel in a Utah airport and reported about him and his wife having dinner. By the end of May, Vrabel held another news conference at offseason workouts and reiterated his devotion to her. "I love Jen," he told reporters.

 But if Vrabel appeared to be under siege, those inside the organization say the team had already moved on.

 

 

 ABOUT TWO WEEKS after the Post published the first photos, Patriots players and coaches gathered for a regularly scheduled meeting, their first since February's Super Bowl loss to the Seattle Seahawks. Some had followed the scandal and seen the photos.

 Vrabel spoke in the same serious tone that he used when addressing the team after a loss, according to a Patriots source. Three players in the room said Vrabel told them he was responsible for creating a distraction and bringing negative attention to the team. He said that challenges always come, but what matters is how people handle adversity when it hits, the players said.

 "He feels like he did wrong by us," Stevenson said.

 Vrabel shared no details about his relationship with Russini, nor did he explain what he'd done to cause the distraction he acknowledged, according to five people in the room. Players asked no questions, and Vrabel quickly moved on to explain the team's schedule for the day before the team broke off into smaller meetings.

 "None of the team was really even worried about specifics," Stevenson said.

 Another Patriots player reached by ESPN, who requested anonymity to speak freely, offered a different perspective: "It's difficult to explain to people outside the building how he approached it and how players took it," he said. "Of course players care about [what happened]. Vrabel is a great leader. Sometimes you have to mess up to become an even better leader."

 But simply addressing the distraction was enough accountability, four players said. "His leadership was never tied to how he lived his personal life," said the Patriots source, who noted that things would be different if Vrabel were a pastor responsible for shepherding souls and exemplifying morality.

 "Ultimately football players care about respect, they care about accountability, and they care if you can make them better," the source said. "And if you can do those things, you can be the weirdest person or you can be a stone-cold killer and they won't care."

 When players have off-the-field issues, a high-ranking executive for another NFL team told ESPN, team brass often discusses whether they should address the team. "And the answer is usually no. Players care about winning games and making money."

 Shaun Smith, a former defensive end who played with Vrabel in the NFL, suggested there could even be a newfound relatability to the coach: "Some guys are gonna be like, 'Hey, he's a dirtbag like me.' You might have some guys who want to high-five him."

 When asked about Vrabel, players and colleagues spoke glowingly about both his coaching and his humanity. He sprints to the tunnel after every game to greet each player coming off the field. He also allows players the space to prioritize their families.

 Byard played for Vrabel in Tennessee, and in 2023, his newborn son spent five months in the hospital. He said Vrabel called…

title: What will Patriots do if RB TreVeyon Henderson is out Week 1?
summary: Henderson did not practice on Saturday, raising some questions about New England's lack of proven depth at running back.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. -- Quick-hit thoughts and notes around the New England Patriots and NFL:

 1. Henderson's status: Running back TreVeyon Henderson played in every regular-season and playoff game during his rookie season in 2025, giving the Patriots a speedy option who was a threat to score on any one play.

 So the uncertainty regarding his status for Wednesday's season opener at the Seattle Seahawks (8:20 p.m. ET, NBC) -- due to an ankle injury that has kept him out of practice since Aug. 24 -- is the type of adversity he hasn't been accustomed to in the NFL. It also sparks a question: If Henderson doesn't play or is limited in what he can do, how do the Patriots handle the running back repetitions?

 Rhamondre Stevenson would have been the clear-cut starter regardless, just as he was last season when he played 46 snaps in the opener to Henderson's 25. Stevenson said he came out of training camp feeling great physically. His knack for blitz pickup has earned him the highest degree of confidence from the coaching staff, with coach Mike Vrabel saying Saturday that "the way he finished last year was exciting."

 "I love the way that Rhamondre protects," Vrabel said early in training camp. "If you have backs that can pick up pressure, it's one thing to be able to get over there and know where the pressure is coming from. It's another [thing] to go block them."

 The only other running back on the 53-man roster is first-year player Corey Kiner , whom the Patriots acquired in a trade from the Arizona Cardinals on Aug. 28 to fill the void created when Terrell Jennings was placed on injured reserve Aug. 13. Vrabel mentioned the Patriots had attempted to sign Kiner ("a good young runner") after the 2025 draft when he instead went to the 49ers. Kiner (5-foot-9, 209 pounds) has four games and 30 offensive snaps of NFL experience, so thrusting him into an expanded role in a frenzied Seattle environment just 13 days after he joined the Patriots would be asking a lot.

 

 That's why Lan Larison (5-11, 209) and/or Hassan Haskins (6-2, 228) have a strong chance to be elevated from the practice squad. Larison, a second-year player from UC Davis, spent last season on injured reserve (foot) after initially signing with the Patriots as an undrafted free agent. Haskins is a four-year veteran who broke into the NFL on Vrabel's Tennessee Titans squad in 2023.

 Larison gets the edge in terms of background in coordinator Josh McDaniels' system (critical with pass protection in mind), while Haskins would be the pick if NFL experience (44 games) was deemed a priority. Both factor into the mix on special teams, especially on punt protection, which is an area the Patriots have spent countless hours practicing throughout the summer.

 "Guys have different strengths. There's a little bit of everything, and we'll see who we end up using for the game," Vrabel said.

 Henderson totaled 911 yards on 180 carries (5.1 average) in the 2025 regular season, with nine touchdowns. He became the first player in team history to have four 50-yard runs or rushing touchdowns in a single season, while adding nine receptions for 35 yards and one touchdown.

 The Patriots focused on their first- and second-down game plan in Thursday's practice without him. And then on Saturday, they worked with full shoulder pads and blocked and hit, according to QB Drake Maye .

 A Stevenson-Henderson one-two punch, with the addition of veteran free agent fullback Reggie Gilliam , had the Patriots feeling good about the potential of the running game throughout training camp. Then Henderson injured his ankle, clouding the outlook for the NFL's opener. 

 2. Thin at OLB: Arguably the biggest surprise heading into the season is how light the roster and practice squad look at outside linebacker, especially with Vrabel saying it wasn't a surprise to him that veteran Harold Landry III is starting the season on the physically unable to perform list -- meaning Landry will miss a minimum of four games.

 Dre'Mont Jones and Elijah Ponder are the starters, with rookies Gabe Jacas (second round) and Quintayvious Hutchins (seventh round) the top backups and Jose Ramirez (four career games played with Buccaneers in 2024) on the practice squad. Asked what he likes about the group on sports radio WEEI, Vrabel noted Jones' veteran presence, Ponder's consistency and then "daily improvement" from Jacas and Hutchins.

 The possibility that Jacas and Hutchins are one snap away from a front-line defensive role is a reminder of how important it will be for the Patriots to avoid injuries, which was a key to their 2025 success.

 3. A.J mentors Jacas: Receiver A.J. Brown remembers how hard Vrabel was on him as a rookie with the Titans in 2019, and he sees some similarities to how rookie Jacas is being coached by Vrabel this year. So, Brown recently approached Jacas to have a chat.

 

 "Vrabel is on him -- really tough. I'll be sitting in my chair laughing, just to see the process and witness it all over again," Brown said. "I don't have any worries for Gabe; he's been locked in. Hopefully my words help."

 4. 'We are firemen': The latest episode of the Patriots-produced "Forged in Foxborough" was released late last week, with the behind-the-scenes look into team meetings and Vrabel's messaging among the notable highlights. Vrabel showed the team boxing trainer Teddy Atlas' "We are firemen" corner speech to amplify the identity he hopes to create. There were also clips of Vrabel calling out Brown and defensive tackle Milton Williams , showing that he holds some of the team's best players accountable in front of everyone.

 The Atlas speech hit home with defensive tackle Leonard Taylor III .

 "It's about staying laser focused to put out the fire," he said. "It's going into this week with a mindset that we need everybody -- you can't put out the fire with just one person."

 5. Gonzo looms: When it comes to cornerback Christian Gonzalez and the Patriots negotiating a contract extension, Vrabel said Saturday that he doesn't get involved in negotiations but takes an active role "in trying to get the situation resolved." He referred to it as a "delicate balance."

 Gonzalez said Saturday that he didn't have anything to share on where negotiations stand, and Vrabel -- who expressed how he wants to coach Gonzalez -- didn't budge when asked if he felt a resolution was close.

 "I think whenever the deal is done, that's when it'll be resolved. I don't have a timetable," Vrabel said.

 6. Crownover's kudos: On the upcoming episode of the "Patriots All Access" show that airs Tuesday on the team website, Vrabel said he showed one play from a 37-13 loss in the preseason finale to the team. It was rookie offensive tackle Dametrious Crownover 's effort following an interception when he sprinted to take out one Browns player before making the tackle. Vrabel noted it came with the team trailing with four minutes left, and that Crownover's play was the type to earn instant respect from veterans.

 

 A sixth-round pick from Texas A&M who is No. 4 on the offensive tackle depth chart, Crownover was pumped to be recognized in front of his peers.

 "We're trying to set a point for our effort and finish -- knowing you're never giving up on a play. In the meeting room, when you get called out by the head coach for that, it's a good feeling," he said. 

 7. Waiver claims : The Patriots were 31st in the waiver claim order after cut-down day, so it was reasonable to expect they would miss out on some of their targets. Turns out they didn't.

 League sources said the Patriots were the only team to put in a claim on the following five players: edge rusher  Jamal Hill (Texans), tight end Cameron Latu (Eagles) and linebackers Shaka Heyward (Bengals), Erick Hunter (Lions) and Darius Muasau (Giants). They were awarded Muasau and Latu, and pulled back their claims on Heyward, Hunter and Hill. They signed Hunter a few days later.

title: NFL's success in Africa has changed scouting process, says Osi Umenyiora
summary: Former NFL star and current coach Osi Umenyiora told ESPN that while in the past, he and his networks had to scout relentlessly for talent in Africa, the success of its recent homegrown stars has led prospects to approach scouts directly.
full_text:
Two-time Super Bowl Champion and head of NFL Africa Osi Umenyiora told ESPN that while in the past, he and his networks had to scout relentlessly for talent in Africa, the success of its recent homegrown NFL stars has led prospects to approach him and scouts directly.

 The 2025 NFL season saw unprecedented success in the regular season from homegrown African talent - and then, in April 2026, Nigeria's Uar Bernard was drafted by the Philadelphia Eagles without playing a snap of competitive football. Bernard was the first African player drafted directly from the NFL International Player Pathway (IPP) program.

 Previously, in September 2025, CJ Okoye had become the first IPP product directly from Africa to play a regular season game. He has since moved from the Baltimore Ravens to the New York Giants .

 

 "I would say so," NFL ambassador and former New York Giants fan favourite Umenyiora told ESPN when asked if scouting networks had significantly deepened in recent years in Africa.

 "On top of that, word is out there now. You know the old saying: 'If you build it, they will come.' Well, we built it and they're coming now.

 "The things that we used to have to do before, we don't necessarily have to do now, because people are reaching out. They're showing us a lot of their videos. They're showing us a lot of stuff.

 "We have people who are interested in the program - a lot of people who aren't even scouts, but they're like: 'Look at this guy, look at this guy, look at this guy.' You know how it is in Africa, so that's how we're getting down right now."

 

 Umenyiora encouraged talented players to reach out to him directly via Instagram, adding: "I'll take a look without a shadow of a doubt.

 "If you don't hear back from me, you already know what that means, but I think everybody should at least make the effort to reach out and see what their abilities are and if they have what it takes."

 He credited Mark Dulgerian for his scouting work for the NFL, which led to the unearthing of talents such as Kenya's Joshua Weru - who has been retained on the Eagles practice squad alongside Bernard.

 Weru picked up a sack in his second ever game of organized football in preseason as the Eagles lost 24-21 to the New England Patriots .

 Before the sack, Umenyiora predicted that the Eagles would take a long-term approach to developing Weru - supported by their subsequent decision not to put him and Bernard in the active regular season roster from the get-go.

 "I first got the videos [of Weru] when he got to the IPP Program, so that's when I first actually understood. I had heard about the kid, but I hadn't seen his training or any of that until he got to the IPP," Umenyiora said.

 "To be fair, he is an explosive, fluid athlete. The numbers he put up to me were extremely impressive... I think if they mould this guy and train him properly, he is going to be a really good football player.

 "It's not going to come overnight, but then, the Philadelphia Eagles are known for developing football players - people who are going to take a while to develop. They're known for that, so I'm happy he went there."

 Three years ago, Okoye had notched a sack in preseason for the Los Angeles Chargers against the Los Angeles Rams . Although it took some time to fully become a mainstay in the league, he is now an established NFL player with the Giants.

 Okoye and fellow homegrown IPP products such as Nigeria's Chukwuebuka Godrick ( Miami Dolphins ) give the likes of Bernard, Weru and other homegrown African stars tangible proof that it can be done.
